traits: Uniform tan, stubbly turf cut down to the stems, often on high spots or uneven ground
Scalped areas are slow to green back up and are more open to weeds and sun stress
Cut appears clean and even, unlike a disease patch or insect damage

copy.what_it_means: Uniform tan, stubbly turf right after a mow, especially on high spots, suggests scalping from cutting too short. Raising the mowing height and following the one-third rule are the realistic fixes; a technician can advise on the right height for your grass.
copy.fact: Removing more than about a third of the blade in one mow stresses the plant enough that it can take weeks to fully recover, even though the cut itself only takes seconds.

tech_notes: Recommend raising deck height and mowing more frequently rather than cutting back hard in one pass; uneven ground often scalps even at a correct average height. Scalped areas are slow to green back up and more open to weeds and sun stress in the meantime.

signs: Uniform tan, stubbly turf cut down to the stems, often on high spots or uneven ground

required_signature.text: A wide photo of the scalped area showing tan stubble cut down to the stems, lined up with high spots or uneven ground.
elements: Uniform tan, stubbly turf cut down to the stems, often on high spots or uneven ground

differentials.difference: Mower scalping is a uniform tan, stubbly cut appearing right after a mow; drought stress shows blue-gray, folded blades across dry zones.
differentials.next_observation: Check whether the discoloration followed a recent mow or a dry, sunny spell.

differentials.difference: Mower scalping cuts turf too short evenly, exposing stems; dull-blade shredding leaves ragged, torn, whitish-brown blade tips at a normal mowing height.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the blade tips checking for a clean short cut versus ragged tearing.

differentials.difference: Mower scalping is a uniform tan cut right after mowing; chinch bug damage expands in hot, sunny spots without a recent low mow.
differentials.next_observation: Pour soapy water on the edge of the patch and watch for small black-and-white bugs climbing up in a few minutes, or a technician checks.

differentials.difference: Mower scalping is a uniform tan cut appearing right after a mow, anywhere in the yard; compaction wear follows a repeated foot-traffic path.
differentials.next_observation: Check whether the thin area is a walking path or matches a recent mow.

condition.recovery_note: Color often returns within 2-3 weeks; density can take 60-90 days at a corrected mowing height.

traits: Blade tips look ragged, frayed and torn instead of cleanly cut
Cut tips look whitish-brown or tan across the lawn
The whole lawn looks dull and grayish-brown from a distance after mowing

copy.what_it_means: Ragged, torn blade tips that turn whitish-brown soon after cutting suggest a dull mower blade tearing the grass instead of cutting it. Sharpening the mower blade is the realistic fix; a technician can point it out on the next visit if you would like a second look.
copy.fact: A torn blade tip dries out and browns faster than a clean cut, and the larger wound is also an easier entry point for leaf-spot fungi.

tech_notes: Recommend sharpening the mower blade frequently enough to prevent tearing of leaf blades; torn tips increase susceptibility to leaf-spot disease.

signs: Blade tips look ragged, frayed and torn instead of cleanly cut
Cut tips look whitish-brown or tan across the lawn

required_signature.text: A close-up of the blade tips showing the ragged, torn cut instead of a clean edge.
elements: Blade tips look ragged, frayed and torn instead of cleanly cut
Cut tips look whitish-brown or tan across the lawn

differentials.difference: Dull-blade shredding leaves ragged, frayed, whitish-brown tips with no lesions; gray leaf spot shows dark-bordered lesions on the blade.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the blade tips versus the lesion pattern.

differentials.difference: Dull-blade shredding leaves ragged, torn, whitish-brown tips with no lesions; melting-out shows distinct brown to purple lesions on the blade.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the blade tips versus the lesion pattern.

differentials.difference: Dull-blade shredding leaves ragged, torn tips at a normal mowing height; mower scalping cuts turf too short evenly, exposing stems.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the blade tips checking for ragged tearing versus a clean short cut.

condition.recovery_note: The lawn's color and texture often improve within a couple of mowings once the blade is sharpened.

traits: Leaf curling, twisting or cupping appearing days to a few weeks after any nearby application
Chlorotic or scorched foliage limited mostly to one area or one side of a plant
Stem die-back or delayed new leaf appearance on a nearby tree or shrub

copy.what_it_means: Curling, twisting or scorched foliage appearing days to a few weeks after any nearby application can suggest herbicide injury. A recent application by anyone, including a lawn service, can cause this pattern; a technician checks what was applied and when before recommending a next step.
copy.fact: Some herbicides can be taken up by tree and shrub roots that extend into a treated lawn, so injury can show up on a plant that was never sprayed directly.

tech_notes: Check timing against any recent lawn or landscape application (by any company); root uptake by nearby trees/shrubs can cause injury without direct spray contact.

symptoms: Leaf curling, twisting or cupping appearing days to a few weeks after any nearby application
Chlorotic or scorched foliage limited mostly to one area or one side of a plant

required_signature.text: A photo of curling or scorched foliage can raise concern, but a technician checks what was applied nearby and when, since a photo alone cannot confirm the cause.
elements: Leaf curling, twisting or cupping appearing days to a few weeks after any nearby application

differentials.difference: Herbicide injury matches where and when something was applied, spot or lawn-wide; iron deficiency stripes the newest blades regardless of any application.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks what was applied nearby and when, and whether the discoloration follows a treated area or a mowing/edging path.

differentials.difference: Herbicide injury matches where and when something was applied, spot or lawn-wide; magnesium deficiency shows blotchy, interveinal yellowing regardless.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks what was applied nearby and when, and whether the discoloration follows a treated area or spreads evenly.

differentials.difference: Herbicide injury often shows curling, twisting or cupping leaves; fertilizer burn shows crisp, brown or yellow turf following a spreader path.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks what was applied nearby and when, alongside the pattern on the ground.

condition.recovery_note: Recovery depends on the product and dose; new growth can look normal within weeks to months once the cause is identified.

traits: Yellow to brown, crisp turf following a straight line or striped pattern matching a spreader path
Damage often appears within a few days of an application, worse at turns, overlaps or spill points
Edges of the damaged stripe are sharper and straighter than a disease patch

copy.what_it_means: Crisp, yellow to brown turf following a straight or striped pattern can suggest fertilizer burn. A recent application by anyone, including a lawn service, can cause this pattern; a technician checks what was applied and when before recommending a next step.
copy.fact: The stripe or overlap pattern is often the biggest clue, since it traces the exact path a spreader took across the lawn.

tech_notes: Check timing and pattern against any recent application (by any company, including overlaps and spill points); watering in unwashed granules promptly reduces further damage.

signs: Yellow to brown, crisp turf following a straight line or striped pattern matching a spreader path
symptoms: Damage often appears within a few days of an application, worse at turns, overlaps or spill points

required_signature.text: A photo of the striped, crisp pattern can raise concern, but a technician checks what was applied and when to confirm the cause.
elements: Yellow to brown, crisp turf following a straight line or striped pattern matching a spreader path

differentials.difference: Fertilizer burn follows a straight or striped spreader path; dollar spot forms small, round, scattered patches with hourglass-shaped blade lesions.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo showing whether the pattern is a straight stripe or scattered circles.

differentials.difference: Fertilizer burn follows a straight or striped spreader path; dog urine spots are round, isolated dead circles with a dark green rim, not a line.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo checking whether the pattern is a straight stripe or a round, isolated spot.

differentials.difference: Fertilizer burn shows crisp, brown or yellow turf following a spreader path; herbicide injury often shows curling, twisting or cupping leaves.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks what was applied nearby and when, alongside the pattern on the ground.

condition.recovery_note: Color and density often improve over a few weeks once the excess is watered through and new blades grow in.

traits: Small, roughly circular dead or straw-colored spot, 3-6 inches across, with a dark green rim around it
Spots cluster in one favorite corner of the yard rather than scattering evenly
The dark green rim fades gradually into normal-colored turf just beyond it

copy.what_it_means: A small, roughly circular dead spot with a dark green rim, especially clustered in one favorite corner, suggests dog urine. Watering the spot well right after your dog goes is the main way to reduce damage; training toward a mulched area helps too.
copy.fact: The dark green ring around a dog urine spot forms because diluted nitrogen reaches the edge of the spot at a level that feeds the grass instead of burning it.

tech_notes: Bermudagrass and zoysiagrass tolerate this better than other warm-season species and often fill spots back in on their own. Female dogs and puppies tend to cause more concentrated spots than males, since males often mark upright over a wider area.

signs: Small, roughly circular dead or straw-colored spot, 3-6 inches across, with a dark green rim around it
symptoms: Spots cluster in one favorite corner of the yard rather than scattering evenly

required_signature.text: A close-up of the spot showing the dead or straw-colored center with a dark green rim around it.
elements: Small, roughly circular dead or straw-colored spot, 3-6 inches across, with a dark green rim around it

differentials.difference: Dog urine spots are small, roughly circular dead patches with a dark green rim and no mushrooms; fairy ring often shows mushrooms and can span several feet.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo showing the full ring size and whether mushrooms are present.

differentials.difference: Dog urine spots are dead circles with a dark green rim clustered near a favorite spot; dollar spot scatters many small patches across the lawn.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo showing whether the spots are scattered or clustered near a dog's favorite spot.

differentials.difference: Dog urine spots are round, isolated dead circles with a dark green rim; fertilizer burn follows a straight or striped spreader path, not a round spot.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo checking whether the pattern is a round, isolated spot or a straight stripe.

differentials.difference: Dog urine spots are small, sharply defined dead circles with a dark green rim; overwatering causes general thin, waterlogged turf without distinct spots.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo checking whether the damage is in small, distinct spots or general across the area.

condition.recovery_note: Small spots often fill back in within a few weeks once watered promptly after each visit.

traits: A scraped, gouged or stripped patch of bark at the trunk base, often ringing part or all of the trunk
Dieback or a thin canopy above a wound that girdles much of the trunk
Damage sits right at grass level where a trimmer or mower deck would reach

copy.what_it_means: A scraped or gouged bark wound at the trunk base, sometimes wrapping part of the trunk, suggests string trimmer or mower damage. A wound wrapping most of the trunk can cut off water and nutrients above it. On a palm this kind of wound never closes; a technician judges the damage.
copy.fact: A wound that rings most of the way around a trunk can girdle it, cutting off the flow of water and nutrients even though the roots below stay healthy.

tech_notes: Estimate the percentage of trunk circumference affected; a mulch ring or trunk guard around the base prevents repeat damage. Palms have no cambium layer, so a trunk wound never seals; treat any trimmer or mower wound on a palm as a possible entry point for disease and have a technician look.

signs: A scraped, gouged or stripped patch of bark at the trunk base, often ringing part or all of the trunk
symptoms: Dieback or a thin canopy above a wound that girdles much of the trunk

required_signature.text: A close-up of the trunk base showing the scraped or gouged bark wound.
elements: A scraped, gouged or stripped patch of bark at the trunk base, often ringing part or all of the trunk

differentials.difference: Trimmer bark damage shows a scraped or gouged wound with bark missing; a mulch volcano buries the trunk base under soil or mulch with no visible wound.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the trunk base checking for a bare wound versus buried mulch.

condition.recovery_note: A minor wound on a shrub or tree often seals over within a season; a palm wound never closes and needs a technician's assessment.
